extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 prior-art exceptions (including common ownership and inventor disclosures), and for using affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 to disqualify disclosures as prior art; includes joint research agreement rules and inventorship correction procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) prior-art exception (inventor/joint-inventor public disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) focuses on the 'subject matter' that had been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No requirement that the mode of prior disclosure by the inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter) be the same as the mode of disclosure of the intervening U.S. patent document; no requirement of verbatim/ipsissimis verbis disclosure. The exception applies only to subject matter in the intervening U.S. patent document that was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor (or someone who obtained it from them) before the date the subject matter relied upon was effectively filed. Example: if inventor publicly disclosed elements A, B, and C, and intervening reference discloses A, B, C, and D, then only element D is available as prior art under 102(a)(2). Species/genus examples: prior disclosure of a species can except a later-disclosed genus; prior disclosure of a genus does not except a later-disclosed species. Determination of applicability of the 102(b)(2)(B) exception is about the subject matter of the intervening document, not a comparison to 'the claimed invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) prior-art exception (common ownership / obligation of assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) excepts subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published document from constituting prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conditions are met, a U.S. patent document that might otherwise qualify as prior art under 102(a)(2) is not available as prior art under either 102 or 103. This differs from pre-AIA 103(c). The 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not apply to disclosures that qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date). Even if a document is not prior art under 102/103 due to 102(b)(2)(C), it may still be used for double patenting rejections or to show state of the art for enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Office rules (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4)/(5)) address commonly owned or joint research agreement subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on usefulness of 102(b)(2)(C) (double patenting and 102(a)(1) exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not remove a U.S. patent document as a basis for a double patenting rejection, and does not apply to disclosures that are prior art under 102(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document excepted from 102/103 by 102(b)(2)(C) may still be cited for double patenting (statutory or non-statutory/obviousness-type) or to indicate state of the art when making a lack of enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If the publication or issue date is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, it may be prior art under 102(a)(1) regardless of common ownership or assignment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of invoking 102(b)(2)(C) — statements and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or the applicant's representative of record) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date will be sufficient to establish that the 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may present supporting evidence (e.g., assignment documents) but is not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence absent independent evidence raising doubt as to the veracity of the statement. Treated analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.130 affidavits/declarations — purposes and types
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.130 provides for affidavits or declarations to disqualify disclosures as prior art under the AIA: (a) affidavit/declaration of attribution under 1.130(a) to show disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or obtained from them; (b) affidavit/declaration of prior public disclosure under 1.130(b) to show the subject matter had been publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained it from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms apply when a claim is rejected as being anticipated or obvious based on a disclosure and the applicant seeks to disqualify that disclosure as prior art under the exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for a 37 CFR 1.130(b) affidavit/declaration (prior public disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 1.130(b) must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and provide the date such subject matter was publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained it from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier public disclosure was in a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must be accompanied by a copy of that printed publication (1.130(b)(1)). If the earlier disclosure was not a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what subject matter had been publicly disclosed on that date (1.130(b)(2)). The manner of disclosure is not critical — differences in mode or wording do not preclude use of 1.130(b) (e.g., slide presentation vs journal article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and sufficiency for 37 CFR 1.130(a) affidavit/declaration (attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 1.130(a) an affidavit or declaration of attribution may be submitted to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor, or that the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'unequivocal' statement from the inventor or joint inventor that they invented the subject matter of the disclosure, accompanied by a reasonable explanation of additional authors, may be acceptable when the author list includes the inventor. However, a naked assertion of inventorship without context, explanation, or supporting evidence is insufficient (see cases such as In re DeBaun and EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen Group of Am.). If a declaration contends derivation by an inventor named in a cited patent/application, a derivation proceeding (§ 42.401 et seq.) may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 need not show enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(a) or (b) need not demonstrate that the disclosure was an 'enabling' disclosure within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1.130 filing must show only that (1) the disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or obtained from them (1.130(a)), or (2) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained it from them before the relevant date (1.130(b)). Enablement is not required for the affidavit/declaration to be effective to disqualify prior art under the AIA exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an assignee, obligated assignee, or person showing sufficient proprietary interest files under 35 U.S.C. 118 rather than the inventor, the inventor may sign the affidavit/declaration but the declaration must be filed by a party having authority to take action in the application. If the inventor is not the applicant, filing authority generally lies with the applicant (not the inventor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations where 37 CFR 1.130 affidavits/declarations are not available
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 are not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; may also be unavailable where the rejection is based upon a U.S. patent or application naming another inventor and the affidavit alleges derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an affidavit would result in the Office issuing or confirming two patents containing patentably indistinct claims to two different parties, 1.130 is not available (see In re Deckler). In such cases, a petition for a derivation proceeding (37 CFR 42.401 et seq.) may be required (1.130(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) joint research agreement exception (common ownership via JRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person for 102(b)(2)(C) purposes if: (1) the subject matter was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is defined as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(h)). To invoke JRA-based common ownership, applicant or representative must provide a statement asserting the three statutory conditions; supporting evidence may be presented but is not required, and the Office will not request corroboration absent independent evidence raising doubt. If the issue or publication date of the cited document is before the effective filing date, 102(a)(1) may still apply regardless of the JRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper naming of inventors — requirements, consequences, and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent laws require naming the actual inventor(s) of the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 115(a)); the Office presumes the named inventors are the actual inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application names a person who is not the actual inventor, the situation should be handled in a derivation proceeding under 35 U.S.C. 135, by correction of inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, or through a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115, as appropriate. Where incorrect inventorship is present, applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48. In rare situations where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventorship and no correction request has been filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Use Form Paragraph 7.04.02.aia and related form paragraphs as instructed for such rejections, and include explanation of supporting evidence in bracketed text of the form paragraph.
